passages.happening:
God tells Moses to leave Sinai and go up to the land he promised to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (verse 1). “And I will send an angel before you, and I will drive out the Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites” (verse 2).

“Go up to a land flowing with milk and honey. But I will not go with you, because you are a stiff-necked people; otherwise, I might destroy you on the way” (verse 3).

“When the people heard these bad tidings, they went into mourning, and no one put on any of his jewelry” (verse 4). “So the Israelites stripped themselves of their jewelry from Mount Horeb onward” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The calf has been destroyed, and the first judgment has passed. But the relationship is not mended. This chapter asks the most serious question of the whole story.

God offers Israel everything he promised: the land, victory, milk and honey. Only one thing is held back. He will not go with them himself. An angel will lead them.

Remember what chapters 25 to 31 were for. The whole plan of the tabernacle existed ‘so that I may dwell among them’ (25:8). Now God says he will not. And the reason he gives is a mercy as well as a judgment. A holy God in the middle of a stiff-necked people would be their death. A stiff-necked people is like an ox that will not bend its neck to the yoke.

The people understand what they have lost. They call the news ‘bad tidings’, though the land is still theirs. They would be given the gifts and lose the giver, and they mourn.

Taking off jewelry was a sign of mourning and repentance. It fits this moment exactly. The calf had been made from their ornaments. Later the people will bring their jewelry freely for the tabernacle (35:22). The same gold can serve an idol or the true God.

‘Horeb’ is another name for Mount Sinai. ‘A land flowing with milk and honey’ describes good pasture for goats and sheep, and sweetness, wild or farmed. The honey may be syrup from dates or grapes, but bees were kept too. Rows of clay beehives from about the tenth or ninth century BC were dug up at Tel Rehov in the Jordan Valley.
passages.later:
Jacob's household once did the same when they gave up their foreign gods: “they gave Jacob all their foreign gods and all their earrings” (Genesis 35:4).

When the tabernacle was built, “all who had willing hearts, both men and women, came and brought brooches and earrings, rings and necklaces, and all kinds of gold jewelry” (Exodus 35:22).
passages.asks: God offered the people the land without himself, and they mourned. Ask whether you would be content with God's gifts if he were not in them. And ask what you would need to take off, or lay down, to show that you mean your repentance.

passages.happening:
“Now Moses used to take the tent and pitch it at a distance outside the camp. He called it the Tent of Meeting, and anyone inquiring of the LORD would go to the Tent of Meeting outside the camp” (verse 7).

When Moses went out, the people stood at their tent doors and watched (verse 8). “As Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would come down and remain at the entrance, and the LORD would speak with Moses” (verse 9). The people would stand and worship, each at the entrance to his own tent (verse 10).

“Thus the LORD would speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” (verse 11). Joshua, his young assistant, stayed at the tent.
passages.hearers:
The story pauses to describe something Moses did regularly. He pitched a tent outside the camp, and there God met him.

This is not the tabernacle of chapters 25 to 31, which has not yet been built. That tent will stand in the center of the camp, with Aaron's priests. This one stands outside, with Moses and Joshua. Readers explain it in two ways. Traditional interpreters take it as a temporary tent Moses used until the tabernacle was finished. Many critical scholars see an older tradition of a tent where God came down to speak, set beside the account of the tabernacle. These notes do not choose.

Its place in the story matters either way. God has said he will not go in the middle of the people. So the meeting place is ‘at a distance outside the camp’. The people who were to have God's house at their center now stand at their own doors and watch one man walk out to meet him. They worship from far off.

‘Face to face, as a man speaks to his friend’ is a Hebrew way of speaking about direct, personal conversation. In that world, to see a king's face was to be let into his presence. Moses was let in. Abraham too is called God's friend.

Joshua, who will lead Israel after Moses, does not leave the tent.
passages.later:
God says of Moses, “I speak with him face to face, clearly and not in riddles” (Numbers 12:8).

James says of Abraham that “he was called a friend of God” (James 2:23).

Jesus said to his disciples, “No longer do I call you servants, for a servant does not understand what his master is doing. But I have called you friends” (John 15:15).
passages.asks: God spoke with Moses as a man speaks to his friend. Ask whether you speak to God as to a friend, or only as to a stranger you need something from. And ask whether anyone watching your life would see where you go to meet him.

passages.t: ‘If Your Presence does not go with us’
passages.happening:
Moses says to the LORD, “You have been telling me, ‘Lead this people up,’ but You have not let me know whom You will send with me” (verse 12). “Now if indeed I have found favor in Your sight, please let me know Your ways, that I may know You and find favor in Your sight. Remember that this nation is Your people” (verse 13).

“And the LORD answered, ‘My Presence will go with you, and I will give you rest’” (verse 14).

“‘If Your Presence does not go with us,’ Moses replied, ‘do not lead us up from here. For how then can it be known that Your people and I have found favor in Your sight, unless You go with us? How else will we be distinguished from all the other people on the face of the earth?’” (verses 15-16).

“So the LORD said to Moses, ‘I will do this very thing you have asked, for you have found favor in My sight, and I know you by name’” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Moses will not accept the land without God. This prayer is the turning point of the whole calf story.

Watch how he prays. He does not plead the people's goodness. They have none to plead. He holds God to God's own words: you said you know me by name, you said I have found favor. Then he widens the request. He began with ‘me’. He ends with ‘us’. He will not take God's favor for himself and leave the people outside it. ‘This nation is Your people.’

The Hebrew word for ‘Presence’ is the word for face. God says, word for word, that his face will go. The same word carries the whole chapter: God's face will go with them, Moses speaks with God face to face, and yet God's face cannot be seen.

Two more words keep coming back: know, and favor. To know, in Hebrew, is more than having facts. It is knowing a person. Favor is kindness that is not owed. Moses' whole case rests on favor God has already shown.

Verse 16 says what makes Israel different from every other people. It is not the land, and it is not even the law. It is that God goes with them. Take that away and nothing that matters is left.

And God says yes. The Bible treats bold prayer that holds God to his promises as something he welcomes.
passages.later:
Matthew gives Jesus the name “Immanuel” and explains it: “God with us” (Matthew 1:23). His Gospel ends with Jesus' promise, “surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

Jesus also takes up the promise of rest: “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).
passages.asks: Moses said he would not go one step without God's presence. Ask what plans you are making that you would go ahead with whether God went with you or not. And ask whether you pray only for yourself, or carry others into your prayer as Moses carried Israel.

passages.happening:
“Then Moses said, ‘Please show me Your glory’” (verse 18).

The LORD answers, “I will cause all My goodness to pass before you”, and promises to proclaim his name before him. “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion” (verse 19).

“But He added, ‘You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live’” (verse 20). “There is a place near Me where you are to stand upon a rock, and when My glory passes by, I will put you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with My hand until I have passed by. Then I will take My hand away, and you will see My back; but My face must not be seen” (verses 21-23).
passages.hearers:
Moses has asked three things, each greater than the last: to know God's ways, to have God's presence, and now to see God's glory.

‘Glory’ is kavod. Its root sense is weight, and so importance and splendor. It is the shining of God's presence, seen in the cloud on Sinai.

Look at how God answers. Moses asks to see glory. God promises to show goodness, and to speak his name. What Moses most needs to know about God is not how bright he is. It is what he is like. The next chapter gives the name in full: compassionate and gracious, slow to anger.

‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy’ is said to a people who have just made a calf. In its setting it is not a word about turning people away. It is God's answer to a people who deserved nothing, telling them that his mercy is his own free gift.

Then the limit. Moses may not see God's face. He is hidden in a cleft of rock and covered by God's hand while the glory passes, and he sees only God's back. This is bold, human language for a God who has no body. God shows himself truly, and he does not show himself fully. Even the hand that hides Moses is a kindness.
passages.later:
Elijah later stood at Horeb while the LORD passed by, and he “wrapped his face in his cloak” (1 Kings 19:13).

John writes, “No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known” (John 1:18). He says of Jesus, “We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

Paul speaks of “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6), and quotes verse 19 when he writes of God's mercy (Romans 9:15).

Revelation ends with the limit lifted: “They will see His face” (Revelation 22:4).
passages.hard:
Did Moses see God face to face, or not?

Verse 11 says the LORD spoke to Moses ‘face to face’. Verse 20 says no one can see God's face and live. The chapter leaves both standing, and it means the reader to think.

Most interpreters explain it this way. ‘Face to face’ is a way of speaking about direct, personal talk. It does not claim that Moses saw all that God is. Numbers makes the same point when it sets Moses apart from prophets who receive dreams and visions. Moses was closer to God than any other prophet, and even he could not look on God's full glory.

The ‘back’ of verse 23 has often been understood, by Jewish and Christian readers, as what can be known of God from his works and from his passing by, as distinct from what God is in himself, which no creature can see. Some Christian writers have gone further and suggested that the one who appeared to Moses was the Son before he became man. Others think that reads too much into the text. These notes take no side.

All agree on this much. The chapter holds together real closeness to God and real limits on what a human being can see of him.
passages.asks: Moses asked to see God's glory, and God showed him his goodness. Ask what you most want to know about God, and whether his goodness would be enough for you. And ask where God has hidden you in a hard season, in a way you only understood after he had passed by.
